response.text:
The Mother

Eliza had been brought up by her mistress, from girlhood, as a petted and indulged favorite.

The traveller in the south must often have remarked that peculiar air of refinement, that softness of voice and manner, so often the particular gift of the quadroon and mulatto women. These natural graces, sometimes with dazzling beauty, and almost always with a prepossessing appearance, were Eliza’s. Such as we have described her is not a fancy sketch, but taken from remembrance, years ago, in Kentucky. Safe under the protecting care of her mistress, Eliza had reached maturity without those temptations which make beauty so fatal an inheritance to a slave. She had been married to a bright and talented young mulatto man, a slave on a neighboring estate, by the name of George Harris.

This young man, hired out by his master to a bagging factory, had, by adroitness and ingenuity, become the first hand in the place. He had invented a machine for cleaning hemp, which, considering the education and circumstances of the inventor, displayed quite as much mechanical genius as Whitney’s cotton-gin. He was possessed of a handsome person and pleasing manners, and was a general favorite. Nevertheless, as this young man was in the eye of the law not a man, but a thing, all these superior qualifications lay under the control of a vulgar, narrow-minded, tyrannical master.

This same gentleman, having heard of the fame of George’s invention, rode over to see what this intelligent chattel had been about. Shown the machinery by George—who, in high spirits, talked so fluently, held himself so erect, looked so handsome and manly—his master began to feel an uneasy consciousness of inferiority. What business had his slave to be marching round the country, inventing machines, and holding up his head among gentlemen? He’d take him back, put him to hoeing and digging, and “see if he’d step about so smart.”

Accordingly, all hands were astounded when he suddenly demanded George’s wages, and announced his intention of taking him home.

“But, Mr. Harris,” remonstrated the manufacturer, “isn’t this rather sudden?”

“What if it is?—isn’t the man mine?”

“We would be willing, sir, to increase the rate of compensation.”

“No object at all, sir.”

“But only think of his inventing this machine,” urged a workman.

“O yes!—a machine for saving work, is it? He’d invent that, I’ll be bound; let a nigger alone for that, any time. They are all labor-saving machines themselves, every one of ’em. No, he shall tramp!”

George stood like one transfixed. He folded his arms, pressed in his lips; a whole volcano of bitter feelings burned in his bosom. His large dark eyes flashed; he might have broken out into some dangerous ebullition, had not the kindly manufacturer touched him, and said, low, “Give way, George; go with him for the present. We’ll try to help you, yet.” The tyrant observed, and inwardly strengthened himself to keep the power he possessed.

George was taken home, and put to the meanest drudgery of the farm. He repressed every disrespectful word; but the flashing eye, the gloomy, troubled brow,—indubitable signs,—showed too plainly that the man could not become a thing.

It was during the happy period of his factory employment that he had seen and married his wife. Much trusted and favored, he came and went at discretion. Mrs. Shelby, with a little womanly complacency in match-making, approved, and they were married in her mistress’ great parlor; her mistress herself adorned the bride’s beautiful hair with orange-blossoms, and threw over it the bridal veil. There was no lack of white gloves, and cake and wine,—of admiring guests to praise the bride’s beauty, and her mistress’ indulgence. For a year or two, Eliza saw her husband frequently; nothing interrupted their happiness but the loss of two infant children, whom she mourned with a grief so intense as to call for gentle remonstrance from her mistress. After the birth of little Harry, however, she had gradually become tranquillized; every bleeding tie and throbbing nerve, once more entwined with that little life, grew sound and healthful,—and Eliza was a happy woman, up to the time her husband was rudely torn from his kind employer, and brought under the iron sway of his legal owner.

True to his word, the manufacturer visited Mr. Harris, and tried every inducement to restore George to his former employment.

“You needn’t trouble yourself to talk any longer,” said he, doggedly; “I know my own business, sir.”

“I only thought you might think it for your interest—”

“O, I understand. It’s a free country, sir; the man’s mine, and I do what I please with him,—that’s it!”

And so fell George’s last hope;—nothing before him but a life of toil and drudgery, made more bitter by every smarting vexation and indignity tyrannical ingenuity could devise.

A very humane jurist once said, The worst use you can put a man to is to hang him. No; there is another use that a man can be put to that is WORSE!
